request.title: Can one source tell us why workers protested?
request.topic: Write a roughly 90-second lesson in exactly 2 scenes for secondary-school history students, using only the supplied fictional source packet. Explain the difference between what a source directly reports and what it can justify about motives. Reach a qualified interpretation, not an invented definitive cause. No equations, no scripted pauses, no fabricated facts or additional sources. A timeline or evidence comparison may help. Do not force a mathematical proof or a single causal explanation.

documents.name: fictional-source-packet.txt
documents.text: All events and sources here are fictional. A factory notice dated 4 May announces a 10% wage cut starting 10 May. A worker diary dated 11 May reports that several workers stopped work and records: "My pay will not cover rent now." A manager letter dated 12 May attributes the stoppage to outside agitators but identifies none. No interviews with other workers, attendance totals, earlier wage records, or additional evidence are supplied.

draft.markdown:
# Can one source tell us why workers protested?

## Beat 1 — What is actually reported?

Content needed: Label the whole packet fictional. Show a date-ordered timeline: factory notice dated 4 May; wage cut scheduled for 10 May; worker diary dated 11 May. Keep the scheduled date visibly distinct from a confirmed event. Show the notice's 10% cut and the exact diary quotation, “My pay will not cover rent now.” Identify the stoppage as reported by the diary. Do not show a causal arrow.

Narration: This fictional packet gives us a factory notice, a worker’s diary, and a manager’s letter. Can they tell us why workers stopped work? Start by separating what each source says from what we infer. The notice announces a ten percent wage cut, starting on the tenth of May. The diary, dated the eleventh, reports that several workers stopped work. Its author writes, “My pay will not cover rent now.” That directly records one worker’s concern about pay. It does not tell us what every worker thought, or establish that this concern caused the stoppage.

## Beat 2 — How far can the interpretation go?

Content needed: Retain the same notice and diary and add the manager letter dated 12 May. Compare each account with the reach of its evidence: diary—one worker's expressed concern; manager—outside-agitator attribution, nobody identified. Show that the announced cut precedes the reported stoppage without making sequence equal causation. Mark the missing evidence from the packet: other workers' interviews, attendance totals, earlier wage records. End with “Pay concerns may have contributed” visibly qualified by “Scale and other motives unknown.” Do not depict agitators as established people or assign motives to the unrepresented workers.

Narration: The manager’s letter, dated the twelfth, blames outside agitators but names none. That records the manager’s explanation; it does not establish that agitators were responsible. Both writers offer limited viewpoints. However, the diary connects pay to a specific concern, rent, while the letter supplies no identified agitators. Together with the notice’s timing, this supports a cautious interpretation: pay concerns may have contributed to the stoppage. We cannot say how widely that motive was shared, or exclude other motives. Without other workers’ accounts, attendance totals, or earlier wage records, the cause remains only partly explained.

prerequisites: Distinguish a historical source from the event it describes.
plan.learningGoal: Distinguish a source's direct report from an inference about motives, and use the fictional packet to state a qualified interpretation with specific limits.
plan.centralQuestion: What can this source packet justify about why workers stopped work?
plan.keyInsight: The diary directly expresses one worker's pay concern, which, alongside the announced cut's timing, makes pay a plausible contributing motive; neither that account nor the manager's unsupported attribution establishes the motives of all participants or a definitive cause.
plan.runningExample: The fictional factory packet: 4 May notice announcing a 10% wage cut starting 10 May; 11 May worker diary reporting several workers stopped work and stating 'My pay will not cover rent now.'; 12 May manager letter attributing the stoppage to unidentified outside agitators.
misconceptions: A source's attribution of a cause establishes that cause.
One worker's expressed concern represents every worker's motive.
An announced implementation date proves the cut took effect as planned.
Events occurring in sequence prove a causal relationship.
Different viewpoints make all claims equally supported.

# Can one source tell us why workers protested?

## Beat 1 — What the sources actually say

Content needed: All material is fictional. Build a dated evidence sequence: notice dated 4 May announcing a 10% wage cut starting 10 May; diary dated 11 May reporting that several workers stopped work and stating, ‘My pay will not cover rent now’; manager letter dated 12 May attributing the stoppage to unidentified outside agitators. Distinguish the date of the diary from an independently established date of the stoppage. Keep all claims attached to their sources.

Narration: Why did these factory workers stop work? Our fictional packet contains three sources, but they do different jobs. A notice dated May fourth announces a ten percent wage cut, starting May tenth. That establishes an announced policy; it does not show anyone’s actual pay.

Narration: A diary dated May eleventh reports that several workers stopped work. Its writer says, ‘My pay will not cover rent now.’ We have a report of a stoppage and one person’s financial concern. A manager’s letter dated May twelfth blames outside agitators, but names none. That records the manager’s explanation; it does not establish that agitators caused the stoppage.

## Beat 2 — From reports to a qualified interpretation

Content needed: Compare what each source supplies with the inference it can support. Preserve the notice’s status as an announcement, the diary’s single-writer scope, and the manager’s unsubstantiated attribution. Reach a qualified wage-related interpretation without treating chronology as proof. Show the limits: no other worker interviews, attendance totals, earlier wage records, or additional evidence.

Narration: The wage explanation has some support: the cut was due to begin before the diary entry, and the writer connects pay with difficulty covering rent. Together, these make financial pressure a plausible contributor to the stoppage. But the diary does not explicitly say why every participant joined, or even that its writer joined.

Narration: The manager offers a competing explanation. Naming no agitators leaves that claim unsupported within this packet, rather than proven false. Without other workers’ accounts, attendance totals, or earlier wage records, we cannot settle everyone’s motives. Our conclusion is qualified: the announced cut may have contributed to the stoppage, while the reasons individual workers took part remain uncertain.

draft.markdown:
# Can one source tell us why workers protested?

## Beat 1 — A report and a possible motive

Content needed: Fictional source packet. A dated evidence timeline distinguishes the 4 May notice from its announced 10 May wage-cut start, and the 11 May diary from the events it reports. Show the diary quotation exactly: My pay will not cover rent now. Keep the interpretation separate from source wording. Preserve notice and diary identities for beat-2.

Narration: On 11 May, a worker writes that several workers have stopped work. Was a wage cut the reason? Our fictional packet offers clues.

Narration: A factory notice dated 4 May announces a ten percent wage cut starting on 10 May. The next day's diary reports the stoppage and says, "My pay will not cover rent now." This directly records the diarist's concern about rent. The timing links that concern with the announced cut, supporting financial pressure as a possible motive. But the diary does not say why every worker stopped.

## Beat 2 — Weigh the claim, limit the conclusion

Content needed: Continue with the same evidence. Add the 12 May manager letter attributing the stoppage to outside agitators, with none identified. Compare what each source reports with what it supports. Reveal the qualified interpretation only with the final spoken block. No other worker interviews, attendance totals, earlier wage records, or additional evidence are supplied.

Narration: A manager's letter, dated 12 May, blames outside agitators but identifies none. It directly shows what the manager claimed; it does not establish that agitators caused the stoppage. Both writers offer partial views. We should neither dismiss the manager's claim nor turn one worker's worry into everyone's motive.

Reveal (spoken): The wage explanation has more specific support: an announced cut, a reported stoppage soon afterward, and one worker's concern about rent. The cut may have contributed to the stoppage. Without other workers' accounts or further evidence, we cannot establish a single cause or all workers' motives. A reported claim and a justified conclusion are different things.
